title: Luke 20
description: Luke 20 in the Liberation and Inclusion Translation (LIT).
topics: give to Caesar what is Caesar’s
paragraphs: 1 One day, while Jesusa was in the sacred grounds teaching the people and bringing the news of triumph,b the lead priests and Scripture scholars, and the elders with them stood up 2 and addressed him, “Tell us by what sort of authorityc you are doing these things! Or who is it who gave you this authority?”
3 He answered them, “I will also ask you something. Tell me: 4 Was John’sd immersione from the heavens or from humans?”

5 They calculated with each other, “If we say, ‘from the heavens,’ he will say, ‘Why didn’t you trustf him?’ 6 But if we say, ‘From humans,’ the entire people will stone us because they’re convinced John was a prophet.” 7 So they answered that they didn’t know where he came from.
8 Jesus told them, “Then I’m not telling you by what sort of authority I’m doing these things either.”
9 Then he began telling the people his parable:

“Someone planted a vineyard, leased it to tenant farmers, and left for foreign lands for a long time. 10 When the time came, he sent someone who was enslaved to him to the farmers, so they would give some of the vineyard’s crop to him. However, the farmers beat him and sent him away with nothing. 11 He tried again, sending another enslaved person. But they beat that one too, humiliated him, and sent him away with nothing. 12 Yet again, he sent a third person, but they drove him out, even wounding this one. 13 Then the ownerg of the vineyard said, ‘What should I do? I’ll send my beloved son. Maybe they will honor him.’ 14 However, when the tenant farmers saw him, they schemed among themselves, ‘This is the heir. Let’s kill him so that the inheritance will be ours!’ 15 So, driving him out of the vineyard, they killed him. Therefore, what will the owner of the vineyard do to them? 16 He will come and destroy those farmers and lease the vineyard to others.”
When people heard this, they said, “May it never be!”

17 Fixing his gaze on them, he said, “Then what is the meaning of what is written: ‘The stone which the builders rejected, that’s the one that became the cornerstone’?h 18 Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and it will crush to bits anyone on whom it falls!”
19 Then the Scripture scholars and lead priests tried to seize him that very hour because they realized he told that parable about them, but they were afraid of the people.
20 Keeping him under close watch, they sent spies pretendingi to be genuine, so they could catch him in something he said so as to hand him over to the jurisdiction and authority of the governor.

21 “Teacher,” they asked him, “We know that you speak and teach correctly. You don’t defer to those of high status but teach the path of God according to the truth. 22 Is it right for us to pay a tribute to Caesar or not?”
23 Perceiving their deviousness, he said to them, 24 “Show me a denarius.j Whose image and inscription does it have?”
“Caesar’s,” they said.

25 He told them, “Then, give what are Caesar’s to Caesar and what are God’s to God.” 26 Confounded by his answer, they kept silent, and they were unable to catch him in anything he said in the presence of the people.

27 Then some of the Sadduceesk (who argue there is no Rising Upl) questioned him. 28 “Teacher,” they said, “Moses wrote for us, ‘If one brother who has a wife dies, and he has no children, then his brother should take the wife and raise offspring for his brother.’m 29 With that in mind: There were seven brothers.n After taking a wife, the first brother died childless. 30 Then the second brothero 31 and the third took her as a wife,p and likewise all seven died without leaving any children. 32 Finally, the woman also died. 33 Whose wife, therefore, will the woman be at the Rising Up? After all, all seven had her as a wife.”

34 Jesus told them, “The childrenq of this Age marry and are given in marriage, 35 but those granted to reachr that Age and the Rising Up from among the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage. 36 In fact, they are no longer able to die because they are the same ass the messengerst and, being children of God, they are children of the Rising Up. 37 But Moses also indicated, in the story of the bush, that the dead are woken upu where it speaks of the Lord as ‘the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.’v 38 God is not the Godw of the dead but of the living since, inx God,y everyone lives.”
39 Some of the Scripture scholars responded, “Teacher, you spoke well!” 40 since they no longer dared question him about anything.
41 But he said to them, “How is it that people speak of the Christz as being David’s son? 42 After all, David himself says in the book of Psalms,

The Lord said to my lord,

‘Sit to my right,

43 Until I put those hostile to you under your feet.’aa
44 Therefore, if David calls him ‘lord,’ how is he his son?”

45 With the entire people listening, he told his students, 46 “Beware the Scripture scholars who want to walk around in fancy robes, who care about deferential greetings in the marketplaces and the seats of honor in the synagogues and the places of honor at meals. 47 They devour widows’ propertybb and pray long prayers as a cover.cc These are the ones who will receive a graver charge.”

footnotes.label: a
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: b
footnotes.html: Traditionally, “preaching the good news.” The word here is a verb euangelizo, meaning to announce or carry the euangelion, traditionally, translated ‘gospel’ or ‘good news.’ The word ‘gospel’ comes from the Anglo-Saxon term god-spell, which means ‘good story.’ The Greek euangelion literally means ‘good message’ and was used specifically of a message announced publicly, which fits the use of the word ‘news.’ The historical context comes from when rulers and military leaders returned to a city after victory in battle, and a herald would be sent ahead to announce the victory and the ruler’s impending arrival. The writers of the Bible took this word and applied it to Jesus’ victory of a different kind. The use of “news of triumph” here is intended to communicate the full meaning of the word in context and not the narrow dictionary definition.

footnotes.label: c
footnotes.html: Or ‘right’ or ‘license’

footnotes.label: d
footnotes.html: The name ‘John’ is the English version of the Latin version of the Greek transliteration (Ioannes) of the Hebrew name Yohanan or in English translations of the Hebrew Bible, Johanan, which means “God has been gracious” or “My God is gracious.”

footnotes.label: e
footnotes.html: In English, translations have traditionally simply taken the Greek word and put it in English letters: ‘baptize.’ The historical reason for this was that the first translators of the Bible into English practiced infant baptism, and the Greek word literally means ‘dip’ or ‘immerse something in a liquid,’ it didn’t fit with their doctrine and practice. Other languages translate it fully, so in Dutch, for example, John is known as ‘John the Dipper.’ In addition to the literal action of dipping or immersing in the water, this is clearly a reference to ceremonial cleansing, preparing people for a sacred calling.

footnotes.label: f
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘believe.’ The Greek term pisteuo communicates meanings such as to trust, to be faithful, to commit, and to give allegiance, reflecting an active, relational endowment of trust rather than a static belief. This translation emphasizes an ongoing, reciprocal relationship between trusting someone and committed faithfulness that confirms trustworthiness.

footnotes.label: g
footnotes.html: This is the word kurios, which is usually translated as ‘lord’ but has other uses depending on context.

footnotes.label: h
footnotes.html: Quotation of Psalm 118:22–23

footnotes.label: i
footnotes.html: This word is the verb form of the one Jesus uses when he calls the religious leaders pretenders or hypocrites.

footnotes.label: j
footnotes.html: A denarius was a Roman coin worth the subsistence wage for one day of labor.

footnotes.label: k
footnotes.html: The Sadducees were a particular sect within Judaism, centered in Jerusalem and composed largely of the priests and those connected with them. They were often quite wealthy and benefited meaningfully from cooperation with the Roman occupation. The theological distinctive especially relevant for this passage is that they did not hold to a doctrine of a future resurrection, which was a major disagreement between them and the Pharisees, and indicates that their question was intended as mocking or a trap, not genuine curiosity.

footnotes.label: l
footnotes.html: This word, anastasis, is the same word traditionally translated as ‘resurrection.’ It can mean something as simple as standing up from lying or sitting. It can also mean to stand up as a public figure entering their role in public view, like a prophet. Here, it points to the Judaic anticipation held by some schools of thought, including the Pharisees, that everyone would be raised to new, physical life at the end of the Age.

footnotes.label: m
footnotes.html: Quotation of Deuteronomy 25:5

footnotes.label: n
footnotes.html: This seems to be an allusion to 2 Maccabees 7, where a mother and her seven sons are executed one after another for refusing to abandon Torah. As each dies, the sons declare that God will raise them to live again. This account became one of the most vivid expressions of resurrection hope of the period and central to debates about whether the dead would be raised. The Sadducees, who deny resurrection, build their scenario on that same scene of seven brothers and serial death, turning a story others told to affirm resurrection into a mocking case against it.

footnotes.label: o
footnotes.html: The word ‘brother’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: p
footnotes.html: The phrase ‘as a wife’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: q
footnotes.html: The Greek is huioi tou aionos toutou. Its most direct translation is ‘sons of this Age,’ but the word huios was also regularly used more figuratively to refer to an heir or descendants more broadly as well as those who were dedicated to following a particular movement or figure and emulating them, or commitment to a way of being and a belonging defined by what they were a huios of.

footnotes.label: r
footnotes.html: The phrase ‘granted to reach’ translates two words. The first, kataxioo, is passive: it describes something done to these people, not something they achieve. It is traditionally rendered ‘counted worthy,’ but in modern English ‘worthy’ suggests earned merit, which the word does not carry and cuts against the meaning of the Greek. Luke uses the same verb in Acts 5:41, where the apostles are granted to suffer dishonor for the Name and rejoice over it. It would not make sense to claim earning dishonor is itself something to celebrate. The word there means being counted as honored by God despite the dishonor from others, not qualifying for it by performance. ‘Granted’ keeps this sense: the reaching is given, not won. The second word, tuchein, had by this period become the ordinary verb for reaching or attaining something, originally having come from the image of hitting the mark on a target with an arrow. The surrounding verses point the same way and suggest there is a theme of belonging here. Some are called ‘children of this Age’ (v. 34) and others ‘children of the Rising Up’ (v. 36), a contrast of belonging to one community and way of life rather than of who has qualified or not.

footnotes.label: s
footnotes.html: The word isangeloi is a compound for ‘the same as/equal to’ (iso-) and ‘messengers/angels’ (angeloi). The traditional renderings typically use ‘like’ which isn’t quite strong enough or ‘equal’ which risks sounding like ‘are at the level of’ which is not what it means. It also does not mean ‘of the same kind as.’ To point toward ‘like’ or ‘of the same kind’ would need to use an entirely different prefix (homoio-). The idea here is that the children of the Rising Up (resurrection) share with the messengers the quality of not being able to die. They are the same in exactly that one way. Some teachings try to say that the messengers don’t marry, which is likely true, but that’s not what the grammar points to.

footnotes.label: t
footnotes.html: The word angelos means ‘messenger,’ sometimes used for spirit beings (as here), but also used for human agents of God (or other people) and sometimes even for natural phenomena. This particular instance seems clearer than most that it is about heavenly beings. It conveys the meaning of someone authorized to speak—or act—on behalf of another. The work of Michael S. Heiser is a great source of information on this topic.

footnotes.label: u
footnotes.html: The word egeiro has several uses. It is one of the words referring to Jesus and others being raised from the dead, and it can mean literally waking up or standing up, as well as being presented as a public figure like a prophet. In cases where it’s referring to being raised to new life, its imagery is the counterpart to the commonly used euphemism of ‘fall asleep’ when referring to someone dying.

footnotes.label: v
footnotes.html: Quotation of Exodus 3:6

footnotes.label: w
footnotes.html: This instance of ‘the God’ is added for clarity. The Greek literally reads “God is not of the dead.”

footnotes.label: x
footnotes.html: Or ‘to,’ ‘for,’ ‘with,’ ‘by’ or several other options. There is no preposition in the Greek, and it must be supplied in English. The more common rendering is to assume ‘to’ which is either so strange as to mean nothing in plain English or implies something like ‘they are alive in God’s perception but not otherwise,’ which would cut against the point Jesus is making that they are alive in some objective sense and not just something like ‘everyone lives in God’s memory.’

footnotes.label: y
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘in him’

footnotes.label: z
footnotes.html: Christos is the Greek translation of the Hebrew meshiah which has traditionally been transliterated as Messiah (and Christ) but translated would literally be “anointed.” The definition of ‘anointed’ is to be ‘smeared with ointment or oil’ and the biblical significance of anointing is to be selected by God (or a prophet of God) for a special appointment, usually king and sometimes other roles like priest or prophet, and experience a ceremony in which the prophet places oil on the head to signify that appointment.

footnotes.label: aa
footnotes.html: Quotation of Psalm 110:1

footnotes.label: bb
footnotes.html: This word most literally means ‘house’ or ‘household’ but can mean the belongings, assets, and resources one has for themself.

footnotes.label: cc
footnotes.html: The word prophasis means ‘a putting forward’ and can be used more neutrally as simply stating the reason for something, but it is often used as something more sinister and loaded. It’s used in 1 Thessalonians 2:5 of a prophasis cloaking greed, similar to this passage. It communicates not just that the prayer is for show but that it is explicitly what hides and enables the predatory behavior.
